key: Four are his horns, three are the feet that bear him; his heads are two, his hands are seven in number. Bound with a triple bond the Steer roars loudly: the mighty God hath entered in to mortals.
s: In a hymn that praises the streams of holy oil poured to Agni, the verse turns to a many-limbed Steer; Sāyaṇa, on 4.58.3, reads it first as the sacrificial Agni: four Vedas for horns, three pressings for feet, seven metres for hands.

evidence.gloss: Although, since the hymn has five deities, Agni, the Sun and the rest, this mantra could be explained in five ways, yet by the method stated in the Nirukta and elsewhere it is explained as referring to Agni whose self is the sacrifice and to the Sun, as making them known. Of this Agni who is the sacrifice, the four horns are the four Vedas, standing in the place of horns (though Āpastamba says the sacrifice is performed with three Vedas, four are named because the Atharvan by itself sets out whole rites). Its three feet are the three pressings, called feet as the means of setting forth. The two heads are the Brahmaudana and the Pravargya. The seven hands are the seven metres.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref 4.58.3, at [353,3]). Sāyaṇa on 4.58.3 says the verse could be read five ways but explains it, after the Nirukta, of Agni who is the sacrifice and of the Sun; on the first reading the horns are the four Vedas, the feet the three pressings (savanāni), the hands the seven metres; he then gives the Sun reading (quarters, three Vedas, day and night, seven rays). The sentence’s ‘first as the sacrificial Agni’ with those three identifications is his, in his order. Wilson note 1 reports the same. Plain sense faithful: 4.58 praises the streams of holy oil (ghṛta) that flow to Agni, and 4.58.3 follows the ‘four-horned Buffalo’ of 4.58.2; no four words of the key verse repeated.
